title: Soma Builds the Perfect Star
subtitle: How a Hoysala general carved a dynasty’s mature vision into a single star of stone
era: Keshava temple at Somanathapura, c. 1268 CE
region: Somanathapura near Mysore on the Kaveri
moral: Patronage can turn service into enduring beauty.

sources.citation: Somanathapura Keshava temple consecration inscription, c. 1268 CE, EC Vol. 5
sources.note: Primary old Kannada record naming Soma Dandanayaka and Narasimha III.

sources.citation: M.H. Krishna, Inscriptions of Somanathapura (Mysore Gazetteer, 1965)
sources.note: Dedicated inscriptional study for the site.
Recent evaluation of Somanathapura as a high point of Hoysala style.

panels.shot: epic wide shot from slightly above, temple complex glowing in evening light with Soma Dandanayaka foregrounded in silhouette

dialogue.text: In 13th-century Hoysala Karnataka, not a king but a battle-hardened general, Soma Dandanayaka, vowed to fix his age forever in stone—and built Somanathapura’s perfect star.

panels.shot: slow push-in from a bird’s-eye over the Kaveri river valley towards a small fortified town

dialogue.text: The inscription names the place clearly—Somanathapura on the Kaveri—and names the man: Soma Dandanayaka, general of Hoysala Narasimha III, riding not to war, but to build.

panels.shot: medium shot at town gate, low angle framing Soma against distant hill temples

dialogue.text: By the 1260s, the Hoysalas had filled Karnataka’s hills with temples. Yet Soma’s record is unusual: here, a military officer, not a king, claims the role of temple-maker.

panels.shot: intimate interior wide, inside a modest hall where plans are spread on the floor

dialogue.text: Hoysala art had reached a mature, intricate form—star-shaped plans, dense friezes, towering shikharas. At Somanathapura, Soma chose that full-grown style as his language of devotion.

panels.shot: ground-level plan view, looking down on chalked star outlines and Soma’s hand placing a central marker

dialogue.text: The inscription speaks of a temple for Keshava, with three garbhagrihas. Soma’s choice is clear: a triple-shrined Vaishnava temple, arranged on a star-like platform, balanced and complete.

panels.shot: dynamic construction wide, scaffolds rising around half-built stone walls

dialogue.text: Block by block, the stellate jagati rose. Unlike some royal projects that remained unfinished, Somanathapura’s enclosure and towers would reach their intended height under Soma’s steady oversight.

panels.shot: close-up profile of Soma and a chief sculptor examining a carved panel

dialogue.speaker: soma_dandanayaka
dialogue.text: These stones must speak clearly of our age, long after we are gone.

panels.shot: low-angle view along the temple base, friezes receding into distance with Soma small in frame

dialogue.text: UNESCO’s modern dossier will call this a high point of Hoysala style. Long before that verdict, Soma insists on legible order—each band a disciplined procession in stone.

panels.shot: interior wide shot of the mandapa under construction, pillars rising like a forest

dialogue.text: Within, the Hoysala taste for ornate pillars and patterned ceilings unfolds. This is mature design—no experimental roughness, but confident repetition and refinement under a patron who cares.

panels.shot: dramatic symmetrical frontal wide of the three shikharas completed, Soma tiny at the base

dialogue.text: Here lies a quiet triumph: unlike at many Hoysala sites where towers fell or were never finished, Somanathapura’s three shikharas stand intact, a rare full expression of the form.

panels.shot: shadowy interior shot of the central sanctum doorway, empty pedestal inside

dialogue.text: The inscription honours Keshava. Today, the main image is gone. We do not know when or how—but the stone record lets us glimpse the moment when that sanctum first came alive.

panels.shot: medium shot inside one lateral shrine with an installed deity, Soma bowing

dialogue.text: Narasimha III, Soma’s lord, leans in records toward Jain piety. Yet his general builds a Vaishnava temple. Hoysala patronage flowed across sects and ranks more freely than modern labels suggest.

panels.shot: close-up of stone inscription panel being carved, Soma overseeing

dialogue.text: On one slab, the consecration record fixes the date and the deed: under Narasimha III, Soma Dandanayaka founds Somanathapura and builds this temple. Service becomes memory, carved in script.

panels.shot: evening courtyard wide shot of the first ritual gathering, lamps glowing

dialogue.speaker: soma_dandanayaka
dialogue.text: May this place guard the grace and the craft of our time.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide, blending past and present with faint modern visitors among ancient carvings

dialogue.text: Centuries pass. The dynasty fades. Yet scholars, travellers, and UNESCO dossiers turn back to this quiet town, praising the clarity and fullness of the Hoysala vision kept here.

panels.shot: final contemplative low-angle close-up on Soma’s carved name in the inscription, fingers of a modern visitor gently tracing it

dialogue.text: Soma Dandanayaka did what many patrons forget: he turned his loyalty and power into enduring beauty, proving that service to a king can also be a quiet service to posterity.
